A tokenizer is the first component of every language model pipeline.
Tokenizers turn text into token ids, and every token id costs money to process.
A good tokenizer learns frequent character pairs so that common words become one token.
Training is simple: count adjacent symbol pairs, merge the most frequent pair, repeat.
The tokenizer must be lossless: decoding the token ids has to give back the text.
Whitespace is information, so the tokenizer keeps spaces inside the tokens themselves.
Determinism matters as well: the same corpus and the same vocabulary size give the same merges.
Unknown characters are rare, but a tokenizer must say what it does with them instead of guessing.
The vocabulary size is a budget, and the merge table is the artefact you ship with the weights.
Encode the text, decode the token ids, and check that nothing changed along the way.
Tokenizers are small, testable components, and they deserve tests like any other component.
The pipeline is only as reproducible as the tokenizer that feeds it, so we version both together.
A tokenizer that loses a space turns a sentence into a puzzle for the model that reads it.
